_doc: Buying guide shown in the app's Supplies tab. Search strings are the deliverable — product links go stale, search terms do not. Set affiliate.amazon_tag to append an Associates tag to every Amazon link from one place; empty means plain links.

affiliate._note: Amazon Associates forbids earning commission on your own purchases, so an empty tag is correct for a personal tool. It is also correct for this REPO: a tag committed here would ship in every fork and earn for the wrong person. Set it in ~/Library/Application Support/Card Studio/my_supplies.json under affiliate.amazon_tag, which stays out of git. Disclose it wherever the guide is republished — the FTC and the Associates agreement both require it.

diagnosis.title: Ink beaded up, smeared, or wiped off?
diagnosis.cause: The card was almost certainly not inkjet-printable. Raw PVC is hydrophobic — it repels water-based ink, so the ink sits on the surface in beads and rubs off with a fingertip. No printer setting fixes this; the card itself has to carry an ink-receptive coating.
checks: The listing must literally say inkjet printable or ink receptive coating. Blank PVC cards alone is not enough.

"Graphic quality" / "premium graphic quality" is a SURFACE GRADE for direct-to-card (dye-sublimation) ID printers — it is not a coating claim. Those cards are normally uncoated and inkjet ink will bead straight off them. This is the most common wrong buy.
Cards sold for card printers usually mean dye-sublimation or retransfer machines. Those are the wrong surface for inkjet.
Laser printable is a different coating again and will not take inkjet ink.
If you can smudge the print with a damp finger after a minute, the coating is missing — not a settings problem.

faq.q: Is there a protective film I need to peel off the card?
faq.a: For pre-cut inkjet PVC cards — no. The ink-receptive coating is bonded to the card at manufacture; there is nothing to remove and nothing to peel. If a card looks like it has a film, that shine is the coating itself. Packs often include thin paper slip-sheets between cards to stop them scuffing in transit — those are packaging, not part of the card.
faq.why_confusing: Search results mix this up with a completely different product: A4/Letter "PVC card making sheets" or "AP Film". With those you print onto a film, peel its backing, heat-laminate it onto a rigid PVC core, then cut the card out. That workflow does involve peeling films — but it is not what you are doing. You are printing directly onto a finished card in a tray.

faq.q: One side looks slightly different from the other. Which side prints?
faq.a: Cards sold as double-sided are coated on both faces, so either works. If a card is coated on one side only, the coated face is usually marginally less glossy and slightly grippier to a fingertip. When in doubt, print a test on one face and check whether the ink dries rather than beads.

faq.q: The ink prints but smudges or scratches off later.
faq.a: That is cure time, not coating. Leave the card 90 seconds before touching the face and 24-48 hours before laminating or heavy handling. Glossy stock holds ink on the surface longer than matte. A light clear acrylic spray sets it if the cards get real-world wear.

faq.q: I want a physical card game — which cards and reader?
faq.a: A game reads cards; it does not need phones to. So 125 kHz EM4100 cards plus a reader is the cheapest path, and the UID is enough — the card's meaning is a row in your table, not bytes on the chip. Use 13.56 MHz NTAG only if a player should also be able to tap a card with their phone. One reader per play zone if zones matter; a PC/SC reader reports UIDs fast enough to use as an input device.
faq.why_confusing: Listings advertise both families as 'RFID' and the cards look identical. They are incompatible, and a 125 kHz card on a 13.56 MHz reader reads as nothing at all.

items.title: 125 kHz EM4100 cards — the no-new-hardware path
items.subtitle: 125 kHz EM4100 — cheapest per card, read-only UID. A PHONE CANNOT READ THESE. Right for a reader-driven card game, wrong for tap-to-open.
items.search: inkjet printable RFID cards 125khz EM4100 CR80 30 mil
specs: The older, read-only-friendly family. Check your reader's listing before buying — many USB readers are 13.56 MHz only, and the two families cannot see each other.
Read-only is fine — your registry binds whatever ID the card ships with, headlessly.
T5577 only if you want to SET the ID
Needs a 125 kHz writer. You do not need one: scan-then-register already works.
CR80 is the size only — it says nothing about what your reader can read.
items.note: The frequency is decided by one question: does a PHONE need to read the card? Yes → 13.56 MHz NTAG. No → 125 kHz is cheaper and a read-only UID is all a game needs, because the meaning of a card lives in your software, not on the chip.

items.title: NTAG215 inkjet cards — $0.17/card
items.subtitle: Timeskey 100-pack $16.95 · needs the dual reader above
items.search: inkjet printable NFC cards NTAG215 CR80 30 mil
specs: NTAG215 (504 bytes) is the common choice — it is what phones and Amiibo/TagMo tooling expect.
This is the phone-readable family. Any modern iPhone or Android can read and write it.
Chip cards are often 0.80–0.84 mm. That is up to 0.08 mm proud of a 30 mil pocket and can jam the tray.
Coil sits in a frame ~8.5 mm wide at the sides, 7.5 mm top and bottom
Turn on the RFID guide in the Design tab — the only guaranteed-flat area is the centred 64 × 34 mm rectangle.

links.label: 100 × inkjet PVC NTAG215 CR-80 (Timeskey)
links.note: Verified 2026-08: 13.56 MHz, NTAG215, CR-80, double-sided inkjet.

items.note: The printing spec on these is correct — explicitly inkjet-printable, CR80, both sides, Canon-compatible. The chip is the catch: NTAG215 is 13.56 MHz, so a 125 kHz-only reader cannot see them at all. Buy these together with a dual-frequency reader, or buy the 125 kHz cards above.

items.title: PC/SC NFC reader — required to write cards
items.subtitle: ACR122U or any PC/SC contactless reader. ~$35. This is the one the Chip tab needs.
items.search: ACR122U NFC reader writer USB PC/SC 13.56MHz
must_say: PC/SC or CCID compliant — this is the whole requirement
read AND write (some listings are read-only)
works with NTAG213/215/216 and MIFARE Ultralight
avoid: "keyboard wedge" or "HID" readers — they type a UID and cannot write anything
125 kHz-only readers — wrong frequency family for NFC cards
phone-only NFC writer apps if you want batch work; fine for one card
items.note: macOS already ships a CCID driver, so an ACR122U works with nothing installed. Reading a card only needs any PC/SC reader; writing needs one that supports transparent APDU exchange, which the ACR122U does.

links.label: ACR122U reader/writer + SDK (Lianshi)
links.note: Verified 2026-08: PC/SC ACR122U. This is the one the Chip tab needs.

items.title: Dual-frequency reader — reads both card families
items.subtitle: Reads both card families as keystrokes — UID only. It CANNOT write a card; pair it with a PC/SC reader if you want the Chip tab.
items.search: dual frequency RFID reader USB 125khz 13.56mhz EM4100 NTAG215 HID keyboard
specs: NTAG213/215/216 + EM4100/EM4305/T5577, 125 kHz AND 13.56 MHz, keyboard emulation
Chip list read off the listing 2026-08-09 — do not buy one that omits NTAG215.
The writer only matters if you want to SET ids; scan-then-bind already makes that unnecessary.
Your 6 existing 125 kHz cards keep working AND NTAG215 starts working — nothing re-bound.

rfid_reader_config.json stores reader_keyboard_types as a LIST, so it can hold both. Expect one --calibrate pass, and check the output format matches the 10-digit convention the dispatcher matches on.
items.note: A dual-frequency reader reads BOTH the 125 kHz family (EM4100/EM4200/TK4100) and the 13.56 MHz family (NTAG213/215/216, MIFARE), so existing 125 kHz cards keep working and commodity NTAG215 stock becomes available. At roughly $22 for the reader plus $17 for 100 NTAG215 cards, 100 cards costs about $39 — versus about $40 for 50 niche 125 kHz cards. If you already own a working 125 kHz reader and only need a handful of cards, this is an upgrade to defer, not a prerequisite.

items.title: Plain inkjet PVC cards
items.subtitle: The everyday card — no chip
items.search: inkjet printable PVC cards CR80 30 mil double sided
specs: Anything else will not sit in the tray pockets.
The tray is cut for 30 mil. Thicker stock rides proud of the pocket and risks a head strike.
Ink-receptive, both sides if you print backs
This is the one that actually decides whether the ink takes.
Matte dries faster and resists smudging; glossy looks richer but needs a longer cure.
items.note: Brainstorm ID is the vendor whose MP-tray template supplied this app's slot coordinates, so their card stock is the closest match to the geometry already loaded.

items.title: Spare 2-card MP tray
items.subtitle: You already have one — this is for a spare or a replacement
items.search: inkjet PVC card tray Canon PIXMA multi-purpose 2 cards
avoid: trays listed only for TS80xx / TS81xx / TS90xx / TS91xx
specs: It drops into the same slot the disc tray uses — that is why the page is 120 × 120 mm.
Both pockets must be loaded every print, even for a single card.
A different tray can shift the slots ~1 mm. Re-run Calibrate if you swap trays.
items.note: If you buy a different tray, run the calibration print again before a batch — the slot coordinates in this app were measured from one particular vendor's tray.

handling: Let cards sit at least 90 seconds before touching the printed face.
Lay them flat in a single layer — stacking wet cards transfers ink to the back of the next one.
Full cure is 24–48 hours. Wait 24 h minimum (48–72 preferred) before laminating.
Keep large solid dark floods out of designs — they pool and dry unevenly on non-absorbent PVC.
